planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this species grows on the same rocky Korean islands as Hosta yingeri but keeps a distinct, smoother-leaved, more upright habit.

directions: This species was formally described from Taehuksan Island off the South Korean coast, where it shares rocky, salt-exposed habitat with its better-known relative Hosta yingeri but is set apart by lighter green, lance-shaped leaves with a smoother texture and a gently undulating margin. Plants form a tight, upright, vase-shaped clump rather than the broader mounds typical of woodland hosta species, and pale lavender flowers appear on tall scapes in late summer. Because of its coastal origin it tolerates leaner, faster-draining soil and more light than most hostas, making it a good fit for a raised rock garden or the brighter edge of a shade bed. It remains uncommon in cultivation and is propagated almost exclusively by division, so expect slow bulking up after planting.
sources: The Genus Hosta (W. George Schmid, Timber Press)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this species comes from Japanese swamps and wet meadows and, unlike most hostas, is unbothered by poorly drained or boggy ground.

directions: Native to the swamps and wet meadows of Honshu, Japan, this diminutive species carries the narrowest, grassiest leaves of any hosta, rarely exceeding about an inch in width, which gives established clumps a fine, strap-like texture quite unlike the broad-leaved garden hybrids. Its low, spreading habit and tolerance for standing water make it a natural choice for pond margins, rain gardens, and bog plantings where typical hostas would rot. Pale purple flowers with contrasting darker anthers open unusually late, from early to mid autumn, extending hosta interest well past the point where most other species have finished blooming. While it adapts to ordinary garden moisture, foliage density and vigor are noticeably better where soil stays consistently damp through the growing season.
